keyVerseText: Woe to thee, Moab! thou art undone, O people of Chemosh: he hath given his sons that escaped, and his daughters, into captivity unto Sihon king of the Amorites.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word כְּמוֹשׁ (Kᵉmôwsh) derives from an unused root meaning "to subdue," conveying the sense of one who conquers or dominates. This etymological background highlights Chemosh as "the powerful subduer," which aligns with his role as a national deity who exercises authority and control over his people. This root meaning enriches the common English gloss by emphasizing Chemosh's character as a god associated with conquest and dominion rather than merely a proper name.
usageInScripture: The term כְּמוֹשׁ appears eight times in Scripture, consistently referring to the Moabite national deity. Translations vary slightly, including phrases like "of Chemosh," "for Chemosh," and simply "Chemosh," indicating possession or dedication to this god. This consistent usage underscores Chemosh's identity as a recognized divine figure among the Moabites and, at times, the Ammonites, with worship practices that even influenced Israelite history, as seen in Solomon's introduction of his high place and Josiah's reforms.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding כְּמוֹשׁ as the Moabite god of subjugation and power provides insight into the spiritual challenges faced by Israel in the Old Testament. Chemosh's worship represented a direct opposition to the one true God, Yahweh, and his presence in Israelite history serves as a warning against idolatry and syncretism. The biblical narrative shows God's judgment on those who follow false gods like Chemosh, affirming the sovereignty of the Lord over all nations and deities. For the Christian faith, this reinforces the call to exclusive devotion to Christ, the ultimate conqueror who subdues sin and death, contrasting with the powerless idols of the world.
keyVerseReflection: Numbers 21:29 declares, "Woe to thee, Moab! thou art undone, O people of Chemosh," highlighting the intimate link between the Moabite people and their god Chemosh. This verse uses the name Chemosh to personify the nation's identity and spiritual allegiance, emphasizing that their fate is tied to this deity. The word כְּמוֹשׁ here underscores the tragic downfall of a people who trusted in a false god rather than the true God, serving as a poignant reminder of the consequences of idolatry.
